blocks.x: The growth nodes

The Winnipeg retail market in 2026 is still growing in several nodes. [Retail Insider's February 2026 review](https://retail-insider.com/retail-insider/2026/02/winnipeg-retail-market-sees-major-investment-wave/) found significant activity across the city:

[**Costco Westport**](https://retail-insider.com/retail-insider/2025/02/costco-opening-in-winnipegs-westport/) opened on November 13, 2025, at about 167,000 square feet. The former St. James location [reopened as a Costco Business Centre](https://retail-insider.com/retail-insider/2026/03/costco-expands-business-centres-across-canada/) on March 27, 2026.

**The Stockyards retail hub,** planned for up to 200,000 square feet in the Water Tower District. In February 2026, construction was expected to begin later that year, after the residential phases start.
**Polo Park,** with new tenants and plans for about 3,700 rental units on its parking lots.
**St. Vital Centre** under new ownership, and **Kildonan Place's $30-million redevelopment.**

New housing adds demand for shops and services in the areas where it is being built. Housing starts rose 40.4% in the first seven months of 2026, the largest percentage increase among Canada's 10 largest cities, the [City of Winnipeg](https://www.winnipeg.ca/news/2026-08-20-winnipeg-leads-major-canadian-cities-housing-growth) reported.
What new Winnipeg retail tenants want
National and regional retailers arriving in Winnipeg often expect:
**A strong storefront** with clear signage, glazing and entrances.
**A clean shell** ready for their own fit-out, or a landlord-delivered turnkey space.
**Durable flooring** suited to heavy foot traffic.
**Accessible entrances and washrooms** that meet code.
**A fast opening date,** because a store earns nothing until it opens, and rent may already be running.
Local and independent retailers often need more help, because they may not have in-house construction teams.
Our view: speed to opening is the hidden competitive advantage

When retailers compare locations, they look at rent, traffic and visibility. But they also look at how quickly they can open. A space that needs demolition and base-building work before fit-out can begin is less attractive than one that is ready to go.
Landlords can gain an edge by investing in **commercial retail renovations** before a tenant signs:
**Strip out previous tenant improvements** so the space shows well, once older materials have been [tested for asbestos](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba).
**Upgrade storefronts and entrances** to modern standards.
**Address accessibility** at entrances and washrooms.
**Repair floors and walls** so the tenant starts with a clean shell.
**Prepare a clear outline of landlord's and tenant's work** for leasing discussions.
Our [vacant storefront renovation guide](/blog/vacant-storefront-renovation-winnipeg) sets out a similar playbook for a smaller unit.

Downtown, the [Storefront Success grant](/blog/how-to-finance-a-commercial-renovation-without-breaking-the-bank) can help businesses in its program area with storefront, façade, lighting, signage, entrance and accessibility work. Its last two deadlines are December 31, 2026 and March 31, 2027, unless funding runs out first. Bridgeland Builders has no role in the program.
Costs and cost control

Construction costs in Winnipeg rose by 4% or more in 2025, say [Altus Group's 2026 Cost Guide insights](https://www.altusgroup.com/insights/caution-in-2026-optimistic-for-2027-cost-guide-insights/). Add higher borrowing costs after the [Bank of Canada's October 2026 hike](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/10/fad-press-release-2026-10-28/), and landlords need to manage renovation budgets carefully. Tactics include:
Standardizing finishes across units to reduce cost and lead times.
Phasing work so revenue starts sooner.
Choosing durable materials that reduce future turnover costs.
Getting written scopes and quotes before committing to tenant allowances.
Questions to ask before marketing a space

Before listing a retail space, landlords should be able to answer a few questions prospective tenants will ask. What is the condition of the storefront and entrance? Is the space accessible? What has to be demolished before fit-out can start? Who pays for what, and how long will landlord's work take?

Does the space suit the uses most likely to lease in the area, whether food, services, medical or retail? A new use can mean a change of use, which starts with a building permit application and then needs an [occupancy permit](/blog/occupancy-permit-change-of-use-winnipeg).

Clear answers, backed by a realistic renovation budget and schedule, make leasing conversations faster and help landlords set rents and [allowances](/blog/tenant-improvement-allowance-winnipeg) that reflect the space's condition.
What to watch

Winnipeg's housing boom should add retail demand in growing neighbourhoods. Watch for new residential projects near your property: the 3,700 units planned at Polo Park, and others elsewhere, could change shopping patterns over the next few years.
Independent retailers need a different approach

National chains usually arrive with design standards and construction teams. Independent and local retailers often do not. For them, a landlord who can offer a turnkey space, or recommend a contractor to deliver the fit-out, makes the decision easier.

Landlords who want local tenants should consider delivering spaces with finished floors, painted walls, updated washrooms and a working storefront, so the tenant only needs to add fixtures and signage. That approach can help fill space in neighbourhoods where national chains are not looking.
The bottom line
Winnipeg retail is growing in specific places. Landlords who prepare spaces for modern tenants, and who get commercial retail renovations done early, are better placed to capture that growth.
